abstract: Subaerial biofilms (SABs) colonizing exposed stone surfaces provide natural systems for investigating microbial community assembly under challenging environmental conditions. Although bacterial diversity on stone has been widely described, whether taxonomic variation reflects broader phylogenetic and ecological differences remains unclear. Here, we characterized SAB communities inhabiting two geographically separated historic urban marble monuments, Federal Hall National Memorial (New York) and the Lincoln Memorial (Washington, DC), using SSU rRNA amplicon sequencing. Additional samples from the Merchants' Exchange Building (Philadelphia) were also examined. Bacterial communities exhibited pronounced taxonomic turnover but substantially greater phylogenetic similarity, indicating that community variation primarily reflected replacement among closely related bacterial lineages rather than turnover among distantly related clades. Despite this taxonomic turnover, core assemblage analyses identified conserved bacterial lineages shared across monuments, several of which were also detected in the independent Philadelphia samples. Consistent with these patterns, inferred ecological composition remained remarkably similar among monuments, with chlorophyll-containing bacteria dominating all communities. Together, these findings demonstrate that these monuments harbor distinct bacterial assemblages while maintaining a conserved phylogenetic and inferred ecological framework, suggesting that environmental filtering and local ecological processes may contribute to SAB community assembly across spatial scales.
